title: From Podolia to the Pampas: the Jewish Gauchos, La Nación, and the Homeland That Is Not a Territory
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: From Podolia to the River Plate

stops.name: Proskurov, the birth in the Pale
stops.date_confidence: contradicted: English and Spanish Wikipedia give 1 January 1883; Jewish Virtual Library and biografiasyvidas.com give 1884, and one of them moves the birth to Tulchin
stops.campa: In Proskurov, a town of the Podolia governorate inside the Russian Pale of Settlement, a son is born to the Gerchunoff household and named Abraham. Two sources give the first of January 1883; two others give 1884, and one of those moves the birth to Tulchin altogether. Neither the year nor the town is settled here, and nothing consulted names a birth house or a street in either of them. The place will be renamed Khmelnytskyi under the Soviets and will end its century inside Ukraine.
suggested_refs: Birth and civil records of Proskurov, Podolia governorate, 1883-1884, unlocated in this pass

stops.name: Proskurov, the house of Rab Gershon
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the father is attested but no date is attached to the household years
stops.campa: His father is Rab Gershon ben Abraham Gerchunoff, a rabbi with traditional Talmudic training, and the boy's first alphabet is read from right to left. Podolia in these years is the old Hasidic heartland; Miedzyboz, where the Baal Shem Tov taught and lies buried, sits in the same governorate. Martin Buber, walking the atlas one province west in Galicia, will spend his working life on tales told in this country and will never travel here to collect them. Gerchunoff is born inside the material Buber will read about in print.
suggested_refs: Rabbinical records of Podolia governorate naming Gershon ben Abraham Gerchunoff

stops.name: Volochysk, the frontier crossed westward
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the year of emigration is attested, this crossing point is not attested for this family
stops.campa: The family leaves. Antisemitic persecution under the tsarist regime is the reason every source gives, and the destination is a colonization scheme in South America underwritten by Baron Maurice de Hirsch. Emigrants out of Podolia bound for a German port crossed the Russian and Austrian frontier near Volochysk; that is the ordinary route of 1889 and it is the only ground for placing the Gerchunoffs on it. No document names this crossing for this household. Taras Shevchenko had walked the same borderlands a generation earlier, and left them under guard.
suggested_refs: Jewish Colonization Association emigration route records, Podolia to the Austrian frontier, 1889
sources: Reconstruction from general JCA emigration route accounts; not attested for this family

stops.name: Bremerhaven, the port without a ship's name
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Spanish Wikipedia states outright that neither a date nor a ship's name survives for this crossing
stops.campa: Spanish Wikipedia puts the matter without softening: for the Gerchunoff crossing there is no date and no name of a ship. The founding cohort of Moisés Ville had sailed from Bremen in August of the same year aboard the steamer Weser, and the Norddeutscher Lloyd emigrant halls at Bremerhaven are the likeliest place to stand a Podolian family bound for Argentina in 1889. Likeliest is not attested. The Weser belongs to the colony's founding story; nothing puts these particular passengers on its manifest.
suggested_refs: Norddeutscher Lloyd passenger manifests, Bremen, 1889
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Alberto Gerchunoff' ('no hay una fecha ni el nombre de un barco')

stops.name: Hamburg, the competing port
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; competes directly with Bremerhaven and is not resolved by any source consulted
stops.campa: Hamburg is the other candidate. Both the Hamburg and the Bremen lines carried Russian Jews to the River Plate in 1889, and the emigrant halls at Veddel processed the same traffic as the Bremerhaven sheds a coast away. Nothing in the record decides between the two. Both ports are entered here and the contradiction is left standing rather than flattened into one embarkation, because the family that crossed left behind no manifest and no letter naming the water they sailed from.
suggested_refs: Hamburg Auswandererhallen passenger lists (Hamburger Passagierlisten), 1889
sources: Reconstruction; contradicts and competes with the Bremerhaven tradition, neither confirmed

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Dársena Sur
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the arrival year is attested, the specific landing record is not located
stops.campa: The Atlantic ends at the old south basin of the port of Buenos Aires, standard point of entry for Jewish Colonization Association settlers of the period. The family disembarks into a city of half a million that is absorbing immigrants faster than it can name streets for them. No arrival record for the Gerchunoffs is located in this pass. Six years from now the boy will come back to this city on his own account and stay in it until he dies; today he passes through it northward, toward a field.
suggested_refs: Hotel de Inmigrantes and Buenos Aires port entry registers, 1889
sources: Reconstruction from standard JCA immigrant routing; specific arrival record not located

stops.name: Rosario, the other landing
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; competes with a direct Buenos Aires routing, unresolved
stops.campa: An equally plausible route sends the colonists up the Paraná to transfer at Rosario before entraining inland for Santa Fe. Both routings were in ordinary use by the Jewish Colonization Association in these years and no document fixes which one this family took. The alternative is plotted rather than suppressed. The destination is documented and the year is documented; the road between them is reconstructed from the habits of the traffic, and the two river ports stand at either end of that reconstruction.
suggested_refs: JCA colonist transport records, Rosario transfer, 1889
sources: Reconstruction from general JCA colonist transport patterns; unresolved contradiction with direct Buenos Aires routing

stops.name: Palacios, the end of the rail
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the railhead is the documented approach to the colony, not documented for this family
stops.campa: Palacios is the nearest station on the Santa Fe line to the new colony, and colonists finished the last stretch by cart across open camp. The family tradition holds that the father described Argentina to them as a promised land where they would farm as the ancient Jews of the Bible farmed. Spanish Wikipedia carries the line as paraphrased family memory and not as a quotation from any document, and it is entered here on those terms. The last miles are made in a cart, which is the vehicle the son will later drive for wages.
suggested_refs: Ferrocarril de Santa Fe timetables and Palacios station records, 1889
sources: Reconstruction from Moisés Ville colony access history
Spanish Wikipedia, 'Los gauchos judíos' (paraphrased family tradition)

stops.name: Moisés Ville, the colony of Baron Hirsch
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The family settles at Moisés Ville in Santa Fe province, a Jewish agricultural colony founded that same year under the sponsorship of Baron Maurice de Hirsch and his Jewish Colonization Association as a refuge from the pogroms. The land was opened to settlement in the decade after Julio Argentino Roca's frontier campaigns brought the pampean and Patagonian territories under national administration; the atlas already walks Roca through Entre Ríos and Choele Choel. Gerchunoff spends part of his childhood here as a farmhand among Russian-speaking Jews learning to ride.
suggested_refs: Jewish Colonization Association colony registers, Moisés Ville, 1889-1891

stops.name: Moisés Ville, the grave in the Jewish cemetery
stops.date_confidence: tombstone date; Spanish Wikipedia states the exact date is unknown, and the research pool contains a contradictory placement of the murder in Entre Ríos which is rejected here
stops.campa: Rab Gershon ben Abraham Gerchunoff is murdered by a gaucho outlaw. The killing happens at Moisés Ville, in Santa Fe, and the grave is in the Moisés Ville cemetery; the tombstone reads the twelfth of February 1891. Spanish Wikipedia adds that the exact date is unknown, which is the whole of its hedge. Two other lenses in the research pool placed this death in Entre Ríos, after the family had moved; that placement is wrong, and the sequence runs the other way. The father dies here, and then they go.
suggested_refs: The tombstone of Gershon Gerchunoff, Jewish cemetery of Moisés Ville, Santa Fe

stops.name: Colonia Rajil, the second colony
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the move follows the father's death of 12 February 1891, so 1891 or later; the coordinate is approximate because no dedicated record of Rajil's position survives online
stops.campa: After the murder the widow moves the household to Colonia Rajil, near Villaguay in Entre Ríos, another Jewish Colonization Association settlement of the same kind. Here the boy works as an agricultural laborer and a boyero, an oxherd, and drives carts for wages through the rest of his boyhood. The coordinate is approximate: no source consulted gives Rajil a position of its own, and every account locates it by naming the nearest town instead. This is the ground that will be written down nineteen years later as Los gauchos judíos.
suggested_refs: Jewish Colonization Association plat maps of Colonia Rajil, Villaguay department, Entre Ríos

stops.name: Villaguay, the town of his lares
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the boyhood years at Rajil run roughly 1891 to 1895 and no source dates a visit to the town
stops.campa: Villaguay is the nearest established town to the colony and the reference point every source uses to place Rajil at all. Thirty-five years later, in a book of essays printed in Buenos Aires, the man apostrophizes it directly, the only Argentine town in his prose that he addresses as a person. The line survives verbatim in the scanned Gleizer edition. The atlas gives the town the coordinate Spanish Wikipedia gives it; a second lens of this research placed it a little south, at -31.9414 and -59.0128, and that discrepancy is recorded rather than averaged.
stops.quote: ¡Oh, Villaguay de mis lares, oh, pueblo dulce entre los pueblos!
stops.quote_source: Alberto Gerchunoff, El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, Gleizer Editor, Buenos Aires, 1926, p. 55 (archive.org scan, leaf 56; printed folio verified against neighbouring leaves)
suggested_refs: The Gleizer Editor first edition of El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, Buenos Aires, 1926
sources: archive.org, El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, OCR full text

stops.name: Villa Domínguez, the hub of Colonia Clara
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the town's role is attested, Gerchunoff's personal presence in it is not
stops.campa: Villa Domínguez, founded in 1890 around the Gobernador Domínguez rail station, becomes the administrative and commercial center of the wider Colonia Clara group in which Rajil sits: the store, the doctor, the telegraph, the Yiddish newspaper. No source places Gerchunoff personally in the town, only in the colony network that ran through it. The stop is entered as the shape of the world the boy moved in, and marked as unattested for him by name, which is a different thing from saying he never went.
suggested_refs: Museo y Archivo Histórico de las Colonias Judias, Villa Domínguez, Entre Ríos
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Villa Domínguez'; personal presence not attested

stops.name: Buenos Aires, arrival at twelve
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Spanish Wikipedia ('En 1895, se traslado a Buenos Aires'); month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In 1895 he moves to Buenos Aires and will spend the rest of his life in it. He is twelve years old. One lens of this research described the move as made by a young man beginning work as a journalist; the arithmetic corrects it, and no source ties the move itself to any employment. No address for the boyhood lodging survives, so the historic center stands in as a symbolic point of arrival. He arrives with the Yiddish of the colonies, the Spanish of the camp, and no schooling anyone has recorded.
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires municipal residence records for the Gerchunoff household, 1895-1900
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Alberto Gerchunoff'; exact residence is a stated gap

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Abraham takes the name Alberto
stops.date_confidence: undated in sources; placed loosely in the years after arrival, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: On acquiring Argentine citizenship he changes his given name from the Hebrew Abraham to the Spanish Alberto. English Wikipedia attests the change and attaches no date to it, so the year here is a placeholder and nothing more. The surname stays exactly as it came out of Podolia, unhispanicized, and it will sit under the masthead of the most respectable newspaper in the country for four decades. Half of him is naturalized and half of him is not, and he arranges the halves himself.
suggested_refs: Argentine naturalization file for Abraham/Alberto Gerchunoff

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the bulletin of Public Instruction
stops.date_confidence: year attested by a single source, biografiasyvidas.com; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He serves as vice director of the bulletin of Argentina's Ministry of Public Instruction. The post is attested by one source only, biografiasyvidas.com, and is not corroborated by Wikipedia in either language or by the Jewish Virtual Library. It is the first documented desk of a working life that will be spent almost entirely at desks with type on them. He is twenty-one, eight years out of a colony in Entre Ríos, and already inside the machinery by which the Argentine state explains itself to its own schoolteachers.
suggested_refs: Boletín del Ministerio de Instrucción Pública, Buenos Aires, 1904 issues

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the literature classroom
stops.date_confidence: undated in sources; the date is a placeholder and the coordinate is a placeholder for two institutions whose addresses were not located
stops.campa: He teaches literature at the Colegio Nacional Belgrano and at the Colegio del Pilar, and serves as vice director of the second. The teaching is secondary-level, not university-level: one lens of this research recorded him as a profesor universitario at an unnamed faculty, and no source consulted supports that. The correction matters because the whole legend of Gerchunoff is a colony boy walking into the institutions, and it is worth knowing which institutions he actually walked into. Neither address was located, and the coordinate is a placeholder.
suggested_refs: Staff registers of the Colegio Nacional Belgrano and the Colegio del Pilar, Buenos Aires

segments.name: La Nación and the Centennial Book

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La Nación at San Martin 350
stops.date_confidence: contradicted: the Jewish Virtual Library dates the joining to 1908, Spanish Wikipedia says only that he began 'muy joven' and gives no year
stops.campa: He joins the staff of La Nación and stays more than forty years, rising eventually to chief editor. The Jewish Virtual Library fixes the year at 1908; Spanish Wikipedia says only that he began very young and declines to give a date, and the two are left unreconciled. The paper is the establishment organ of the Argentine oligarchy, founded by a former president, and the man now writing in it learned Spanish herding oxen. Emin Arslan, the Druze emir without a consulate, will be printing him in La Nota within a decade.
suggested_refs: La Nación staff records and bylines, Buenos Aires, 1908-1950

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the colony stories begin to appear
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Spanish Wikipedia; month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Individual stories out of his colony childhood start appearing in La Nación, one at a time, in the pages a general readership opens on the tram. They are not presented as ethnography and not as testimony. They are simply printed among the other stories, in the ordinary way, by a paper whose readers had no reason to expect that the pampas contained Jews on horseback. Two years of this will be gathered into a book. The critic Perla Sneh will later call the resulting dialect an improbable gaucho literature of the exile.
suggested_refs: La Nación, Buenos Aires, 1908-1910, the colony stories as first serialized

stops.name: La Plata, Los gauchos judíos is printed
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted; publication in La Plata does not by itself prove personal travel to the city
stops.campa: Los gauchos judíos is published at La Plata as a tribute to the centennial of the May Revolution: twenty-four stories, drawn from a boyhood in Moisés Ville and Rajil, offered to the nation on its hundredth birthday by a man who had arrived in it at six. The Encyclopaedia Judaica will call it the first Latin American work to treat Jewish emigration to the New World and the first work of literary value written in Spanish by a Jew in modern times. Borges will argue two decades later that Argentines stand to Europe as Jews stand to the West.
stops.quote: an improbable Gaucho literature of the exile
stops.quote_source: Critic Perla Sneh on Gerchunoff's blend of Judaeo-Spanish and gauchesco dialect ('gauchesca de un desterrado'), as translated in English Wikipedia from Gerchunoff and Sneh, Los gauchos judíos: El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, Ediciones Colihue, 2007, p. 21; the Colihue original could not be loaded to confirm the Spanish wording
suggested_refs: The 1910 La Plata first edition of Los gauchos judíos, twenty-four stories
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Alberto Gerchunoff' and 'The Jewish Gauchos'

stops.name: Madrid, the lecture at the Ateneo
stops.date_confidence: attested by a single source, biografiasyvidas.com; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He lectures at the Ateneo de Madrid during travels in Europe. One source carries this, biografiasyvidas.com, and no other consulted source mentions the trip. It is worth naming because a second lens of this same research asserted flatly that no source places Gerchunoff in Europe as an adult, while citing this very page elsewhere for the Ateneo. Adult travel to Europe is attested, thinly, by one source, and the internal contradiction inside the research pool is reported rather than quietly deleted.
suggested_refs: Ateneo de Madrid lecture programmes, 1914

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El nuevo régimen and Cuentos de ayer
stops.date_confidence: years attested (El nuevo régimen 1918, Cuentos de ayer 1919); months and days defaulted; the two titles are carried as one stop
stops.campa: Two books inside two years: the essay collection El nuevo régimen in 1918, and Cuentos de ayer in 1919. He is by now a working man of letters with a newspaper behind him, publishing at the rhythm of a columnist rather than a novelist. In these same years he is politically active in the Progressive Democratic Party and uses his journalism to attack the caudillismo he associates with President Hipólito Yrigoyen. The colony boy has become a partisan of institutions against personal power, which is a position with a cost.
suggested_refs: First editions of El nuevo régimen (1918) and Cuentos de ayer (1919), Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El cristianismo precristiano
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the title and 1920 date rest on biografiasyvidas.com alone and are uncorroborated
stops.campa: He publishes the essay collection El cristianismo precristiano. The volume is attested by one source only and is entered as unconfirmed. Its subject is the one he returns to for the rest of his life: the Jewish ground under the Christian house. Six years later, in another book, he will stage the circle of Caiaphas discussing an itinerant preacher and write the sentence below, which is his own authorial prose and not dialogue in any character's mouth. Sigmund Freud, in the atlas, worked the same seam from the far side of the Atlantic.
stops.quote: El pálido predicador de Nazareth era para ellos uno de esos profetas iracundos y tristes, que voceaban en la plaza del Templo sus pronósticos agoreros y sus salmodias llorosas.
stops.quote_source: Alberto Gerchunoff, El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, Gleizer Editor, Buenos Aires, 1926, p. 98 (archive.org scan, leaf 99); the quotation is from the 1926 volume, not from the 1920 book this stop names
suggested_refs: El cristianismo precristiano, Buenos Aires, 1920, first edition unlocated in this pass
sources: archive.org, El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, OCR full text

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La jofaina maravillosa
stops.date_confidence: contradicted: Spanish Wikipedia's bibliography and Open Library give 1922, the Jewish Virtual Library gives 1923; 1922 is followed here as the majority reading
stops.campa: La jofaina maravillosa appears, the wondrous washbasin, an extended meditation built around Cervantes. Two sources date it to 1922 and one to 1923, and the majority reading is followed with the minority named. The Quixote will not let him alone: he had written Nuestro Señor don Quijote in 1913 and will leave a Retorno a Don Quijote unpublished at his death. A man who learned Spanish in a cart on the Entre Ríos camp spends his maturity annotating the founding book of the language he acquired.
suggested_refs: La jofaina maravillosa, Buenos Aires, 1922 first edition; the 1927 reissue

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, Gleizer Editor
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the imprint of the scanned first edition; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Gleizer Editor prints El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, the one book of his whose text this research could read directly rather than in citation, page by page, from a scan. The essays move between Athens and Jerusalem without choosing, and the sentence below is the hinge of the argument: two founding peoples, two separate gifts, neither reducible to the other. He is a Jew writing in Spanish for a Catholic country about the Greek and Hebrew halves of its inheritance, and he does not pretend to be a neutral party.
stops.quote: Grecia ha creado en la humanidad la aspiración de la belleza y ha construido la filosofía; los judíos la encendieron en la esperanza y concretaron el concepto de la misericordia.
stops.quote_source: Alberto Gerchunoff, El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, Gleizer Editor, Buenos Aires, 1926, p. 124 (archive.org item elhombrequehablo0000albe, OCR full text; diacritics restored where the scanner misread them)
suggested_refs: El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, Gleizer Editor, Buenos Aires, 1926, first edition
sources: archive.org, El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, OCR full text (item elhombrequehablo0000albe)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, page thirty and what a homeland is not
stops.date_confidence: same volume and same year as the preceding stop; the page citation was corrected from an initial reading of p. 90 to the printed folio 30
stops.campa: On the thirtieth page of the same volume he defines a homeland by subtraction. Not the territory, not the army, not the particular motion of a country's law or its economy: it is that, he writes, and something more, outside the graspable, escaping the coercion of philosophical formulas. The man writing is a Russian-born Argentine who will spend the 1940s campaigning for a Jewish state he does not intend to move to. The research pool had this quotation at page 90; the scan puts it at printed folio 30, and the citation is corrected here.
stops.quote: La patria no es el territorio, no es el Ejército, no es el movimiento peculiar de su legislación o de su economía.
stops.quote_source: Alberto Gerchunoff, El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, Gleizer Editor, Buenos Aires, 1926, p. 30 (archive.org scan, leaf 31, printed folio verified on the page itself)
suggested_refs: El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, p. 30, the essay on patria
sources: archive.org, El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, OCR full text

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the same page and the language of dreams
stops.date_confidence: same page as the preceding stop, a few lines below it; both were initially mis-cited to the nineties
stops.campa: A few lines further down the same page he asks the question that answers the definition. Why do we not dream in a foreign language; why do we not throw the cry of indignation or of joy in the words we learned coldly, as a science. He is a man whose first language was Yiddish, whose sacred language was Hebrew, and whose entire published work is in Spanish, asking in Spanish which language the involuntary parts of him still use. The essay gives no answer that this reader could find on the page.
stops.quote: ¿Por qué no soñamos en lengua extranjera? ¿Por qué no lanzamos el grito de indignación o de regocijo en los vocablos que hemos aprendido fríamente como una ciencia?
stops.quote_source: Alberto Gerchunoff, El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, Gleizer Editor, Buenos Aires, 1926, p. 30 (archive.org scan, leaf 31, same page as the preceding quotation)
suggested_refs: El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, p. 30, on mother tongue and patria
sources: archive.org, El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, OCR full text

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Martín Fierro called an anarchist
stops.date_confidence: same volume; the page citation was corrected from p. 168 to the printed folio 174 after the scan's leaf-to-folio offset was found to shift mid-book
stops.campa: Late in the volume he turns to the gaucho as a political figure and notes that the poets who found their inspiration in the gauchesco conceived the countryman with an identical sense of subversion. Then the sentence below. Sixteen years after putting Jews on horseback in the Argentine national imagination, he is arguing that the national poem itself was always a poem about a man the state wanted arrested. Roca's army had cleared the camp these figures ride across, and Gerchunoff's family farmed what it opened.
stops.quote: El comandante del regimiento llama anarquista a Martín Fierro, el héroe del más admirable poema de América.
stops.quote_source: Alberto Gerchunoff, El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, Gleizer Editor, Buenos Aires, 1926, p. 174 (archive.org scan, leaf 173; offset fixed against printed folios on leaves 167, 168 and 174)
suggested_refs: El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, p. 174, the essay on the gauchesco
sources: archive.org, El hombre que habló en la Sorbona, OCR full text

segments.name: The Editor and the Society of Writers

stops.name: Madrid and Buenos Aires, the book on Heine
stops.date_confidence: imprint year attested in the bibliography; the joint imprint does not establish personal travel for this edition
stops.campa: Enrique Heine, el poeta de nuestra intimidad carries a joint Buenos Aires and Madrid imprint. Gerchunoff writes about the German Jew who converted, who was banned, and whose lines the Germans kept singing anyway as folk songs by an unknown author. The subject is not accidental for a man who took a Spanish first name and kept a Podolian surname. Whether he crossed for this edition is not documented; that he had lectured in Madrid thirteen years earlier is attested by one source, and the two facts are not joined here.
suggested_refs: Enrique Heine, el poeta de nuestra intimidad, Buenos Aires and Madrid, 1927
sources: Spanish Wikipedia and English Wikipedia, 'Alberto Gerchunoff' (bibliography, joint imprint)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the direction of El Mundo
stops.date_confidence: attested by a single source, biografiasyvidas.com; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He directs the newspaper El Mundo. The paper is a tabloid founded two years earlier by the Haynes group, aimed at a mass readership on the tram rather than at the readers of La Nación, and he runs it while remaining attached to La Nación across the whole of his career. One source carries this and no other consulted source corroborates it. The colony boy is now an editor in chief in a city where the Jewish immigration is still recent enough to be a subject of newspaper argument.
suggested_refs: El Mundo, Buenos Aires, mastheads of 1927 naming its director

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the founding board of SADE
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the claim that he was SADE's first president is rejected here as an error of the Jewish Virtual Library
stops.campa: The Sociedad Argentina de Escritores is founded and Gerchunoff sits on its first comisión directiva. The Jewish Virtual Library calls him the society's first president; Spanish Wikipedia's article on SADE gives that office to Leopoldo Lugones and places Gerchunoff on the board. The conflict resolves against him and it is recorded that way rather than left open. He is a founding board member, which is what the record supports. Twenty-four years later the same society will give him its highest prize, and he will be dead.
suggested_refs: Acta de fundación of the Sociedad Argentina de Escritores, Buenos Aires, 1928
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Gerchunoff, Alberto' (claims first president; treated as an error)

stops.name: Azul, Las imágenes del país
stops.date_confidence: imprint year attested in the bibliography; whether the imprint reflects a personal visit is not established
stops.campa: Las imágenes del país is printed at Azul, an inland town of Buenos Aires province, rather than in the capital: an unusual imprint among his works and the only one of its kind. Whether this records a journey out to the camp or simply a provincial press arrangement is not established by anything consulted. The title says the images of the country, and the country in question is the flat one, four hundred kilometres from the port, where the images he keeps returning to were originally seen from the seat of a cart.
suggested_refs: Las imágenes del país, Azul, 1931, first edition and its printer
sources: Spanish Wikipedia and English Wikipedia, 'Alberto Gerchunoff' (bibliography, imprint Azul 1931)

stops.name: Montevideo, El hombre importante crosses the river
stops.date_confidence: imprint year attested; personal travel across the river for this edition is unconfirmed
stops.campa: The novel El hombre importante is co-published in Buenos Aires and Montevideo. Traffic across the Plate was ordinary for writers of his circle in these years, though no source confirms he crossed for this edition. Victoria Ocampo had launched Sur from her house at San Isidro three years earlier, gathering the same literary establishment that Gerchunoff, as a senior man at La Nación, moved through daily; no direct link between them turned up in any file consulted, and the shared milieu is inference and not attestation.
suggested_refs: El hombre importante, Buenos Aires and Montevideo, 1934
sources: Spanish Wikipedia and English Wikipedia, 'Alberto Gerchunoff' (bibliography)

segments.name: The Turn: Hitler, Zion, and the Colonies Remembered

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Once, the end of assimilation
stops.date_confidence: year attested as the turning point; the shift is described by sources as a process rather than a dated event
stops.campa: Hitler takes power in Germany and Gerchunoff changes position. The man who had spent twenty-three years arguing that Jews belonged in Argentine rural life by farming it turns to the preservation of Jewish culture as such, and to Zionism, and to organized resistance against antisemitism; he joins antifascist intellectual groups including AIAPE and works out of the Jewish civic and press networks around Once. Nothing he wrote before 1933 is repudiated. The argument simply acquires a second half that the first half had not needed.
suggested_refs: AIAPE (Agrupación de Intelectuales, Artistas, Periodistas y Escritores) membership records, Buenos Aires, 1930s

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Los gauchos judíos in twenty-six stories
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Spanish Wikipedia; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Los gauchos judíos is reissued with two further stories added, twenty-six in place of the original twenty-four. The book that had been a centennial offering in 1910 is now reissued in a decade of European catastrophe, and the colonies it describes are no longer a curiosity of the pampas but the surviving alternative to what is happening in the countries the colonists left. He does not rewrite the earlier stories. He adds to them, which is a different operation, and lets the new context do the rest.

stops.name: Santiago de Chile, La clínica del doctor Mefistófeles
stops.date_confidence: imprint year attested; personal travel across the Andes for this edition is not documented
stops.campa: La clínica del doctor Mefistófeles is published at Santiago de Chile, his only Chilean imprint. As with Azul and Montevideo and Madrid, the imprint is documented and the journey is not. Four foreign or provincial presses across ten years describe a writer whose books travel more reliably than his body does, or whose body travelled and left no record of it. The distinction is not decidable from anything consulted, and the stops are plotted where the type was set rather than where the author is known to have stood.

stops.campa: Between roughly 1945 and 1948 he campaigns among Latin American political leaders on behalf of Jewish statehood, work the Jewish Virtual Library credits with contributing to the bloc of Latin American support that will matter at the United Nations. He is in his sixties, a newspaper editor with forty years of standing in a country whose foreign ministry reads his paper. Martin Buber, in the atlas, is in Jerusalem arguing for a binational state; Gerchunoff is in Buenos Aires counting votes.

Whether that means a body in New York or letters and pressure routed through Argentine delegates is not distinguished by the source, and it is not resolved here. segments.name: Entre Ríos, mi país: the Last Book and After

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Entre Ríos, mi país
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the book appears in the year of his death and the month is not fixed by any source consulted
stops.campa: The autobiographical Entre Ríos, mi país is published, the last book, and its title gives a province of Argentina the word country. He had been born in Podolia, had crossed an ocean at six, had lost his father to a gaucho at eight, and had spent fifty-five years in the capital. The homeland he names at the end is not the empire he left, not the state he lobbied to create, and not the city he worked in. It is the camp near Villaguay where he drove oxen as a boy.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the death of Alberto Gerchunoff
stops.date_confidence: attested; some catalog metadata alternately lists the death year as 1949, and the age of sixty-seven depends on the 1883 birth date rather than the 1884 one
stops.campa: He dies in Buenos Aires at sixty-seven, an age that holds only if the birth year is 1883 rather than 1884; a scattering of catalog metadata puts the death in 1949 instead. No source consulted names the neighbourhood, the residence, or the hospital, and the city-centre coordinate stands in for a site not recovered. Borges, who is walking the same city in the atlas, will put the assessment below on him: a writer beyond dispute whose fame was of another order than a writer's.
stops.quote: Fue un indiscutible escritor, pero el estilo de su fama trasciende la de un hombre de letras. Sin proponérselo y quizá sin saberlo, encarnó un tipo más antiguo: el de aquellos maestros que veían en la palabra escrita un mero sucedáneo de la oral, no un objeto sagrado.

stops.campa: The Sociedad Argentina de Escritores awards him its Gran Premio de Honor, and he is the only writer in the history of the prize to receive it posthumously. He had sat on the society's first board twenty-four years earlier, when Lugones was president and the honour was not yet invented.
